activities.anchor: Copper mined in 1900 came from ore grading about
activities.caption: drag the divider — the ore of 1900 against today's
activities.name: oreGradeCompare

config.prompt: What could be paid for is the whole story — drag the divider between the two mining worlds:

before.text: Copper ore grading 2–3 percent — the rich deposits, mined when the technology and prices of the day could pay for nothing leaner.

after.label: Today
after.text: Large copper mines work rock near 0.5 percent — neither number reflects how much copper exists, only what technology and prices could pay for.

config.why: Mining engineering begins as an economic geology problem: the grade moved because markets and machines did — reserves rise and fall with prices.

activities.anchor: products of a few great concentrating engines
activities.caption: file the famous deposits by the engine that made them
activities.name: oreEngineBuckets

config.prompt: Three engines concentrate metals — file each deposit under its engine:
buckets: magmatic segregation — gravity sorting in cooling magma
hydrothermal circulation — hot brines moving metal
sedimentary and surface processes — water, weather and time

items.label: Bushveld Complex platinum — a layered intrusion the size of a small country
Sudbury nickel-copper — the melt sheet of an ancient asteroid impact
porphyry copper — vast low-grade zones above cooling magma chambers
volcanogenic massive sulphides — metal-rich mounds on ancient seafloors
epithermal gold — fluids flashing near the surface
placer gold sorted into river gravels
banded iron formation — chemical sediments in Precambrian oceans
bauxite — tropical rain leaching ordinary rock

config.why: Learn the engines and you can predict where to look: gravity in slow magma, brines along heat gradients, density and weather at the surface.

activities.caption: pair each style with the setting it builds
activities.name: oreHydroMatch

config.prompt: One mechanism produces most of the metal mines on Earth. Pair each style with its setting:

pairs.right: vast low-grade zones (0.3–1% Cu) above cooling magma chambers
where those fluids flash near the surface
metal-rich mounds precipitated on ancient seafloors
fractures filled with quartz and sulphides

config.why: The common thread: metal once spread through cubic kilometres of ordinary rock was dissolved, moved, and re-precipitated into a small volume.

activities.name: orePlacerPlace

config.why: Gold's density is 19.3 g/cm³ against rock's 2.7 — the same physics behind the California and Klondike rushes.

activities.anchor: ore does not look like metal
activities.caption: true or false — seeing modern ore
activities.name: oreInvisibleJudge

statements.s: Modern gold ore is often grey rock with no visible glint.
statements.why: A few grams of invisible gold per tonne, locked inside sulphide minerals at scales below what the eye can resolve.

statements.s: Nevada's Carlin-type deposits are named for the large nuggets found there.
statements.why: They are named for microscopic gold — and are among the most productive gold fields on Earth.

statements.s: 'Shiny nugget' geology died in the 1800s; exploration now targets what an assay reveals.
statements.why: Today's targets are things a microscope or an assay shows — not the eye.

statements.s: If you cannot see metal in a rock, it cannot be ore.
statements.why: Almost nobody who has seen modern gold ore in a photograph believes it — the value hides below the eye's resolution.

activities.anchor: Exploration is a funnel run on scarce capital
activities.caption: stack the funnel — cheap before expensive
activities.name: oreFunnelOrder

config.prompt: The professionals' first skill is deciding where NOT to drill. Order the funnel:
items: Desktop studies: regional geology, past workings and remote sensing pick the belts
Geological mapping on the ground: outcrops, alteration haloes, structures
Geochemistry: stream sediments, soils and rock chips hunt the halo around hidden ore
Geophysics: magnetics, gravity, EM, IP and gamma-ray read the rocks through cover
Drilling: RC chips or diamond core — confirmation, not exploration
config.why: Everything cheaper happens first; drilling is the most expensive way to learn anything about the subsurface.

activities.anchor: measuring physical properties from the air or ground
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the survey plan
activities.name: oreGeoSpot

config.prompt: A junior company's survey plan for a massive sulphide body hiding under cover contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Deposit model: a massive sulphide body hiding under cover, no outcrop.
Fly magnetics to map magnetite-bearing rocks, intrusions and alteration.
Gamma-ray spectrometry will find the sulphide body through 100 m of cover — it maps potassium, thorium and uranium at the surface.
Drill only the anomalies that survive the triage.
config.correction: Gamma-ray spectrometry maps potassium, thorium and uranium at the surface — reading alteration and lithology; it does not see a buried sulphide body through cover.
config.why: Each method discriminates on a different property, so the choice encodes the deposit model.

activities.anchor: Now run the headline numbers on a worked example
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the worked deposit
activities.name: oreStakesEstimate

config.prompt: The worked example: 20 million tonnes of ore at 3 grams of gold per tonne. How many tonnes of gold does the deposit contain?
config.why: 20,000,000 × 3 g = 60 tonnes — about 1.93 million troy ounces, roughly $3.9 billion in-situ at $2,000/oz.
config.context: At ~90% recovery and $1,100/oz operating cost, the pre-tax margin is about $1.7 billion over an eight-to-fifteen-year mine life.
